mcqs.question: Given `order.getCustomer()` returns a `Customer`, why does `order.getCustomer().getAddress()` already violate the Law of Demeter?
options: It doesn't violate anything — the Law of Demeter only restricts chains of four calls or more
It's a syntax error in most object-oriented languages
Address is only accessible through a private field, so this line won't compile
Address is reached through Customer, an object the caller doesn't directly hold — the caller now depends on a "stranger" two hops away
mcqs.explanation: The Law of Demeter is about how many objects deep your code needs to understand, not chain length in calls — reaching to Address through a Customer you only obtained via order.getCustomer() already couples the caller to a stranger. There's no fixed threshold of calls, this is valid syntax, and nothing here implies a compile error.

mcqs.question: Code does `if (account.getBalance() < amount) throw new Error(); account.setBalance(account.getBalance() - amount);` at three different call sites. What does Tell, Don't Ask recommend instead?
options: Replace all three call sites with a single account.withdraw(amount) method that enforces the rule internally, so it can't be forgotten or reimplemented inconsistently
Add more validation to each of the three call sites to be extra safe
Cache the balance in a local variable at each call site to avoid repeated getBalance() calls
Nothing needs to change — this pattern is already correct
mcqs.explanation: Tell, Don't Ask means pushing behavior to the object that owns the data: an account.withdraw(amount) method keeps the balance rule in one place, enforced consistently. Adding more scattered validation or caching the balance locally doesn't fix the root problem — the rule is still reimplemented at each call site and can drift.

mcqs.question: After refactoring `order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCountry().getTaxRate()` into `order.getTaxRate()` (with Order privately delegating internally), what happens if Country is later replaced with a TaxJurisdiction class?
options: Every caller of the tax rate needs to be found and updated
Only Order.getTaxRate() needs to change; every caller stays untouched since they only ever called order.getTaxRate()
The refactor must be undone since Order shouldn't know about Country either
Customer needs to be updated to know about TaxJurisdiction directly
mcqs.explanation: Since callers only depend on Order.getTaxRate(), the internal traversal change (Country to TaxJurisdiction) is isolated to Order's implementation. Order is allowed to know its own immediate collaborator (Customer) and delegate further internally — that's the point of moving the traversal inside a method the caller trusts.

mcqs.question: A developer sees `order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCountry()` and fixes it by adding `getCustomerAddressCountry()` to Order, which just calls the same chain internally. What's wrong with this fix?
options: Nothing — this is exactly the recommended fix for a train wreck
It mechanically relocates the chain by one level and adds a pass-through method that doesn't express real behavior, rather than giving Order an owned capability like getTaxRate()
It will cause a runtime exception because Order doesn't own an Address
It violates the Interface Segregation Principle
mcqs.explanation: Mechanically wrapping the chain without asking what capability Order should actually own just relocates the train wreck and multiplies pass-through methods across classes. The better fix names the real capability (getTaxRate()) rather than relaying an object-graph path deeper. This isn't an ISP concern, and nothing here causes a runtime failure.
